utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I begin with cross-examination, I wish to inform you that yesterday, at 6.30 in the evening, an associate of mine came, Mr. Tomanovic, to inform me that the order of witnesses has been changed again, yet again, and that another two witnesses were added. Mr. Walker was scheduled for today, and then this current witness was added and then two more witnesses were added last night. And I think that this is an attempt to minimise the time allotted to me to cross-examine Walker, and I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will ensure that that is not the case. Mr. Nice, can we be assured that there will be ample time to hear Mr. Walker?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is absolutely no intention to deprive the accused the opportunity to examine Mr. Walker. My principal focus at the moment is on ensuring that we can find a way of taking Mr. Walker's evidence in chief as shortly as possible, by consideration of possible application of 92 bis to parts of it. The other two witnesses to whom he refers, the witnesses who I think are 92 bis witnesses, crime-base witnesses, they have been here a long time already and there was considerable difficulty in retaining them any longer. That's the difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Provided there's sufficient time for Mr. Walker, no harm will be done. Yes. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, please, can you tell me, how can you explain that at 6.30 two witnesses were added and I was informed of it by my associate? Do you have an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not going to debate it with you, Mr. Milosevic. We have a list. We were told one thing. There has been a change of plan. There's nothing sinister in that. Our task is to ensure that no injustice is done. No injustice is done to you so far. We will ensure you have sufficient time to cross-examine Mr. Walker. Now, let's go on with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are describing not only the events in Bela Crkva but also outside of it, because you also mention events in Nogavac, in Mala Hoca, in Velika and Mala Krusa; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bellacerkva, in Celine, and Nagavc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that this activity of yours took place precisely at the time when there was fighting going on between the forces defending the country and the terrorist forces of the KLA and while the bombing was going on as well, so in view of that, did you perhaps try to show those who were killed during the bombing and in that fighting as somebody who was a victim of a Serb crime, as you describe it?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no KLA in Bellacerkva ever, and all the victims were civilians. There were more than 70 victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you claim that there were no civilian victims in the fighting between the KLA and the police and that there were no civilian victims of the NATO bombing. Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no KLA, and there was -- they were all civilians. There was no fighting between the KLA and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In your statement, on page 1, you say that you lived in a compound in which there were four houses. One house was yours, two of your brothers, and one of your parents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We lived with my brothers, and all four houses belonged to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many people lived in your household?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 22 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you go on to say that you were a truck driver; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been a truck driver, a farmer, and a shepherd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you were a truck driver, you frequently moved or travelled through the municipality. So I suppose that you were well-informed and well -- you were familiar with the circumstances in Kosovo; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only travelled during the vegetable season, between July and September, and otherwise I was involved with livestock on the Sharr Mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But at any rate, you moved about. And just now you told us that there was no KLA in your village, whereas on page 2, paragraph 4 of your statement, it says that there were some in your village. There were, in fact, three members of the KLA there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no KLA units in our village. They were separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not referring to units. You mentioned three individuals. A previous witness from your village, Isuf Zhuniqi, claimed that there were no KLA members at all in your village, and what I'm interested in is what is the precise number of KLA members in your village. Could you help us, please.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no village called Zhuniqi, but it is a family called Zhuniqi. They were individuals who were involved in units of the KLA who were further away, up to 15 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say "village." I said that the previous witness claimed -- let me repeat. I didn't mention the village. I mentioned your fellow villager, Isuf Zhuniqi, who claimed that there were no KLA in your village. And can you tell me where this unit of yours was stationed? These three people that you mentioned were apparently members of the unit that was stationed 15 kilometres away. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let us deal with that fairly for the witness. He has not -- just a moment. He has not accepted that there was a unit. He said specifically there was not a unit in the village. In your statement, Mr. Popaj, you refer to three members of the KLA in the village whom everybody knew. Now, those three members, where were they stationed in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They weren't in the village but were in KLA units in Retia. I've heard about them, because I didn't actually see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So these KLA units that you just mentioned, where were they based?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there at the unit, but I've heard that this unit was at Retia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who was the commander of that unit?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understood your answer to be that you don't know. But in your statement, on page 2, you say that no member of your family belonged to the KLA and that you, just as the majority of residents in the city, provided food and also gave funds to whom? Who did you give the money intended for the KLA? Who did you give this to?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only our village, but all Albanians helped the KLA with food.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about that. What I'm asking is: Who did you turn this over to, the food and the money?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They handed it over to the representative of the village. I was a farmer and a shepherd at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To the representatives of the village. And what was your monthly dues in terms of food and money? I'm referring to the dues that your family was supposed to hand over.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't give money. I gave flour and meat and what I wanted to give.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was your monthly dues?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't give monthly contributions, but we gave when we wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when was that? Was it due once a month, every three days, once a week?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're guilty of what is called suggestio falsi, and you do it all the time. The witness has made it quite clear that he was not required to give anything; he gave voluntarily. But you insist on using the word "dues." That really is a misrepresentation. Please stop it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to raise separately the question of the relevance of this material. I realise that there's reason for not confining an accused who is representing himself too narrowly, but really, these questions about the KLA have got nothing to do with the case, in my respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the answer is this: that there is a very broad relevance in the sense that it is part of the case of the accused that the KLA were responsible for atrocities; indeed, it appears the suggestion that they may be responsible for the ones with which this witness deals, or certainly some atrocities. In those circumstances, he is entitled to cross-examine about it. However, we make it plain that his time is limited because of the way in which time is wasted generally in this sort of cross-examination by him, and therefore the approach of the Trial Chamber is to allow cross-examination, provided it has some relevance, but to limit it in terms of time. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you in Bela Crkva in 1998?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 18th of May and until July, I was within the Sharr Mountains, with cows and sheep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the rest of the time you were there. All right. Do you know who Xhelaj Hajda [phoen], nicknamed Toni, is?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He's not someone from our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was the KLA commander for the Orahovac region?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a different question. I'm asking you: Do you know who the Orahovac region KLA commander was? And you are telling me that you don't know who Hajda was? Does this in turn mean that Hajda was the commander?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the KLA attack on Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know anything about this, and I haven't written about it in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And these three members of the KLA that you mention in your statement, did they participate in the attack on Orahovac, together with others?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: How should I know? I wasn't their bodyguard to accompany them everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell me who -- do you know who Skender Hoxha is?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And during the time when you worked as a truck driver, as a seasonal truck driver, did you also transport weapons or other supplies for the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, in 1998 I wasn't even in the village. I was with the livestock in the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you were in the mountains during the summer, as you said yourself, but the majority of the year, you were in the village, weren't you? Where were you during the rest of the year?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at home, looking after my sheep. I was with the flocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that on March 25th, at 2.00, when NATO started bombing, you went into the basement of your house, together with your family. This can be found on page 2, last paragraph of your statement. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we heard the sound of the Serbian tanks entering the village, when the NATO bombing, Serbian positions above the village started firing. My family and I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about this part of your statement where you say that on March 25th, at 2.00, when NATO started its bombing, you went into the basement, together with your family. Is that right? I didn't ask you about tanks. I asked you about what you stated yourself in your statement.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard the NATO bombing starting at 10.00 at night. But at 2.00, Serbian forces started firing, and then my family and I went to the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read you the last paragraph of your statement on page 2. It says as follows: "When the NATO bombing commenced, my family moved down into the basement of the house." Let's continue on. Was your village bombed by NATO?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't bombed by NATO, nor were we frightened of NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you claim that not a single bomb fell in the vicinity of your village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at Bellacerkva or on Xerxe or on the villages around did a single NATO bomb fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about anyplace in Kosovo where any bomb fell?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. He's giving evidence about his own village and so any broad question is not for him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the tanks came into the centre of the village and then withdrew from the village and took up positions on the hill above the village. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs entered the village at 2.00 and some tanks took positions then. Then from the 22nd of March, there had been tanks there before on a hill above Fetush Hill. And on the 25th more entered at 2.00 in the morning, and some went in the direction of Celine, a place called the hill of Breganoli [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain the following: Were the tanks in the village during the bombing or after the bombing they took up positions on that hill?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 22nd of March, two days before the bombing, they took up position under the home of Nahit Fetoshi and evicted the inhabitants of that house from the house, and these people came to my house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You were asked about the position of the tanks during the bombing. Can you tell us where they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course I can. The tanks were positioned on a hill in the direction of Celine, and there were two armoured vehicles in the schoolyard. The others went to Celine, but I don't know how many there were because it was night and I couldn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the police started shooting from the bunkers above the roofs of the houses and that you and other residents of the village started leaving the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We started leaving the village at 4.00 in the morning when they started burning houses. They started at one end of the village. And I didn't leave my home because all 80 members of my family in the yard, and then we set off to go to Rogova. I went back to my house to let the livestock loose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that perhaps a conflict between the police and the KLA when they entered the village, when you claim that they entered the village?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that the KLA didn't exist. There was no KLA in my village. I told you before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But on page 3, paragraphs 2 and 3, you say that the police was shooting over the tops of the houses to a target that was apparently on the opposite side if they were shooting over the tops of the houses, the roofs of the houses. So who were the police shooting at?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police came up. Had police -- the police had positions on the 22nd of March, and 80 per cent of the people had already left, and they started burning the houses of the people who had left at 5.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In that same paragraph on that same page, you say that you saw Serb forces opening fire on houses as they entered the village, and you go on to say that the policemen used gasoline and flame-throwers. But despite of that, you came back to the village to feed your livestock because you didn't want to leave them unattended. Didn't you state that?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went back to feed my livestock while the houses were burning. And you could hear gunshots. And afterwards, when I had fed the livestock, I went through the other houses and I heard children crying, being mistreated. And then I found the family of Clirim Zhuniqi and Xhemal Spahiu, from Opterusha, with 30 members of his family, and I helped them to cross the river, which was deep. And they were fighting from positions above the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I've understood that from your statement. I did not ask you that. Tell me, is it logical for you in a situation when, you had put it, the police was setting the village on fire, was it logical for you to return only to feed the cattle while they were setting the village on fire?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't leave the village, but I saw the people off, and I helped them to leave the houses and to go in the direction of the Cergova [phoen]. I didn't leave the village. I looked after the village and I saw how the people were setting fire to the village. And after that, I came out of the house and heard the voices of the children, which were 300 metres far from the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A little while ago you said that you heard shooting at that very same time. Where did you hear the shooting?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the shooting from 2.00 a.m. until the time when they were executed, the family of Clirim Zhuniqi and my family all. They didn't stop the shooting until the evening in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who were they shooting at, then, in the evening, in the village? Or rather, were they shooting all over the village all day?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All day they were setting fire to the village. They didn't do it only for one day, but they did it for one month in succession, displacing the people and dispossessing the people of their clothes and setting fire to the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So for a month they were torching your village and shooting all over the village every day?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it has been, because the last house was set to fire on the 4th of May. There were 300 houses in our village, and only 6 houses were not set fire to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who set these houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These houses were set on fire by your police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who were they shooting at all over the village for an entire month?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no people there. They were just shooting at random. They were dispossessing the houses of the clothes. And there were three trucks which were taken by the Serbs, and I have found these trucks in the place called Kllokot, and I found my truck, which the others were taken by the corps police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just tell me one thing: Who were they shooting at when there was no one in the village?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the village, they killed the cattle. There were 5.000 cattle in the village, and none of them remained alive. All the cattle was executed, just like the people were executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many people did they kill in the village while they were shooting during that one month?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people were killed on the 25th of March, and the other days there was nobody in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many of them were killed on the 25th of March?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 25th of March there were killed 70 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where did you see them kill these people?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... to the execution. I've seen them killed because I was there helping the family of Clirim Zhuniqi and Xhemal Spahiu. I was there with the electric pole, and there was near a place for watering, and I was 80 metres far from there. And there I saw the police going in the direction of the Belaja bridge, where the people were executed there. Five persons of my family were executed there, and the sons of my uncle. There were executed 40 persons, civilians, who, after one hour, I came back with my wife and we went to the place of the event, and we saw them executed, my sons, Shendet, and here I have the photograph. I have the photograph of my son when I buried him. You see him all in blood. Here are the two sons. And I have here the witness that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him finish.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And here I have the documents of the son of my uncle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So what is your assertion? How many people were killed or how many people lost their lives then? Forty or seventy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He says 70.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All in all, in this village, there were 70 people killed. I can also quote them with names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Since you mentioned that you saw 12 policemen in different uniforms and some kind of surgical gloves -- is that correct? That is in paragraph 5 on page 3.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On my part, I was on the right side of the river. I have seen 12 police. Whereas on the left part of the river I haven't seen how many police were there, and they were paramilitary from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question you were asked was about the plastic gloves. Is it right the police were wearing plastic gloves that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were not plastic gloves. We found the gloves after we returned, and they were seen by the investigators of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say, precisely, in this paragraph that I've been quoting to you: "Some of them, or most of them, wore bands," et cetera, et cetera. And finally, there is a sentence saying: "All of them were wearing tight-fitting, white plastic-type gloves like those used by doctors." So you claim that you saw policemen wearing plastic gloves, the type used by doctors.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not me who said this, but I have met Zhuniqi with his mother, who were hidden, when they were executed, and they told me that there in Celine and Bellacerkva they saw the people with the gloves, and there they have found the gloves and needles, and they told us about this when they came back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. On the basis of what I read, it was my understanding that you were describing what you had seen. But since you had not seen this yourself, we can proceed. Because this is the first time we hear that police or the military wear surgical gloves. On page 4, paragraph 2, you say that these, as you had put it, policemen, killed those 14 persons whom you had helped. Did you see them kill them?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they were executed, I saw them. I saw the police when they executed them, and after they left, 100 metres from the place where they executed the people, I went to that place and I saw the people being executed. I went there soon after 20 minutes in the event, and then I left because I couldn't stay there. And I started walking towards the railway which takes you up to Prizren. When I approached the railway, I heard shots from the police, from the mill of Xerxe. I fell there and I stayed there. And then I saw my wife, who was taken to the rails of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. railway, and she told me that my sons, my brothers, and everyone who was there was executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popaj, I'm very sorry if you lost your sons, but are you sure that they lost their lives during an execution, or did they lose their lives in a war conflict between any kind of warring parties? It's not even important what particular warring parties.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you felt sorry, you wouldn't have accomplished this deed. But this is true, because I went there. I found eight of them. And there was Alban Popaj, the son of my brother; Feim Popaj, the son of my uncle; Defrim Zhuniqi. And I took six of them to Hysni Popaj. In the evening, Hysni Popaj died in the village at the house of Abaz Kryeziu. And Alban Popaj died on the 26th, at about 1.00, whereas I buried them at 3.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Please, how many people were in that group there by the bridge, underneath the bridge? Because you and the previous witness have been speaking about the same group of people. How many people were there?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some people -- how many people have been all in all, I don't know, but I know how many of them were killed because I have buried them with my own hands and I have written the names of every one of them when I started burying them. Twenty-seven of them. There was a massive graveyard, 36; the other had 2; and the other 2 in the village Xerxe. Whereas the other group of 100 metres [as interpreted], there were 6: the priest of the village, the dervish of the village, and the two sons of my uncle, Agim and Medi Zhuniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that all the time you were by some other people. Doesn't it seem illogical to you that you were along with different people all the time, while you left your own family on the other side?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't been with other people. First of all, I was alone, and then I joined my wife and my father and my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, please: Even then, during these clashes, is it your claim that there was no KLA anywhere while this shooting was going on and everything else that was going on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To pick up His Honour Judge Robinson's point, the accused is doing it again. There's no evidence of clashes. There is evidence of execution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That's right, Mr. Milosevic. What the witness is saying is that these were executions. There was no question of the people dying as a result of some conflict. Now, have you got anything else you want to put to him?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course I do, but the point is that I cannot assume, even assume that it could be an execution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's his evidence which we're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I understand that. I understand that that is what he is speaking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since the police were present all the time in the area during the drive and as the tractors were returning when you went to help the wounded, did your people have any problem with the police? So you took a tractor to pick up the wounded and you refer to that, and you say you were driving back and the police were there. Did you have any problem with the police?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police had left after they did the execution, and they went in the direction of Celine. They were not present. For the truck, there was my wife who went there. And with the truck there came Shemsedin Kelmendi and Abaz Kryeziu, and after that, there came my wife accompanied by other women. And we took all those who were alive - because we were not able to take the victims - but we took the people who were alive to save their lives, and there were eight of them. And we took them to the village Xerxe. I just showed the names to them. It was Alban Popaj, the son of my brother Remzi Popaj, Defrim Zhuniqi, and some others, and we took them to the house of Abaz Kryeziu in Xerxe where his daughter was a nurse there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Popaj. You say that you went to Zrze and that you bought some plastic foil and blankets. This is on page 6. Is it possible that shops are open in a situation where the police, as you had put it, were going about executing all Albanians?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shops were not open, but it was -- on the 27th, all day I went where I could find people in the agriculture stores, and I took the things there. And I waited all day during the 27th. I made two metres of that. And I prepared some glass bottles to write the names. And in the evening, 27th, about 9.00 p.m., there were some co-villagers of mine and some of my friends to help me. And we went at 9.00 in the evening to start burying 36 persons in the massive graveyard. And this is what is written in my declaration. I remember it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Popaj. You don't have to explain things so extensively. Among the names of the victims, you mentioned Jusuf Popaj as well. Do you know according to documents, Jusuf Popaj, on the 17th of May, 1998, was mistreated by the KLA on the road between Malisevo and Orahovac near the village of Dragobilje when a pistol was taken away from him and nine bullets as well and that he personally reported that incident to the police? Do you know about that, since you are related?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a big lie of yours. This is a big lie created by you, because Jusuf Popaj was 70 years of age. He was a hoxha.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am talking about a document that we have, but let us consider what you've said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You've got about two minutes left, Mr. Milosevic, so you should tailor your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tailor it? In terms of two minutes? That's quite difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that in the village of Nogavac - that is on page 10 - that you searched the houses that were destroyed by the bombing, and you say that the bombing of Nogavac was carried out by a Serb plane rather than by NATO. What is your basis for claiming that?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That night from the village Xerxe, we started going with Nazim Rexhepi to the village of Celine. And then when we entered Celine, there came two aeroplanes which flied very low. And then after some minutes, I heard four explosions of bombing, and I didn't know where this explosion fell. But after three days, I heard about the right place where this exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you on the basis of what do you claim that that was or those were, as you said, Serb aeroplanes, not NATO. So even -- so Serb planes were even bombing their own territory, as you had put it.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's because when I went there, I have heard there were many people stationed there who were shooting. But we found pieces of the explosion. We hid them. And KFOR took these pieces. And there were letters there in Cyrillic alphabet. I found in Nagavc the sister of my father killed there, and I buried her on the 6th of April. Her name was Sanije Kastrati.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many people were killed in that bombing?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There I don't know the exact number, but I saw that there were killed eight children and three women. There were -- I couldn't stay there for longer. Then I left. I saw the children there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Milosevic, your time is now finished. Mr. Tapuskovic, have you any questions of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have only two questions precisely related to what is mentioned on page 10, paragraph 4 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when you came to the actual site, you said, this is the last sentence of that paragraph: "The roof tiles and windows in most of the houses in the village were broken by the explosions." Does that mean that these houses, that the majority of the houses in the village were not hit at all and yet were without any windows or roofs? Does that mean that there was a strong gust of air that blew them away?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You speak about the village Bellacerkva or the other village, Nagavc? I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about Nogavac, because you said that you went there the very next morning. The very next morning with Gazmend Malsori and ten other men, you went to the actual site and you saw that on the houses there were no roof tiles and that there were no windowpanes.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were, because of the bombardment, all the tiles which had fallen on the floor. All of them, like the earth was trembling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more thing. In that village, did you see any craters that the bombs had made?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found some pieces, pieces from the bombs when we found the children. We found the pieces of the bombs right there. Was it from the bomb or what else? We don't know. These pieces were taken by the KFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you. Did you see big craters ten metres wide or, rather, ten metres long and seven metres wide? Did you see them? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went there, I saw the people killed, and I took the people out, and I didn't see anything else. Because with my own hands I have buried 168 civilians in the village Bellacerkva, Celine, and Nagavc. I couldn't see anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The photograph that you produced is of your two sons, and I thought you found them on one of them when they were buried; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that's why it's covered in blood. Just help me with this: Was it normal for the son on whose body it was found to carry a photograph of him and his brother or not?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My little son Agon was there with this photograph when I buried him. And perhaps before they parting he wanted to take the photo with him as a souvenir in the moment when the village was set to fire. And you can still see the stains of the blood. This is the photo of my two sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't ask that it be produced as a Court exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Second point: Your statement does say, that is the statement that you signed, it does say at paragraph 3 -- page 3 that when you were looking at the 12 policemen at the side of the Belles stream, that they had particular uniforms, and you give the colours, and that your statement does go on to say, this is you speaking, apparently: "All of them were wearing tight-fitting white plastic-type gloves like those used by doctors." Can you tell us please, just so that we know how to deal with the statement, did you see that through binoculars or otherwise or not? And if not --

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that with binoculars, the 12 police from my side, on the right side. On the left side, I didn't see how many police were there. And I saw them through binoculars.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With gloves?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw -- I saw them executing the people at the Belles bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see them with gloves or not?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had gloves. And they took off the gloves in the middle of the village Celine and Bellacerkva, and we found them afterwards when we made the unburial of the people. I handed them over to the investigators of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those are the only questions I ask in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Popaj, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, while you're changing over and we're just waiting for the witnesses, towards the end of the week, probably on Friday, we would wish to have a further discussion about the witness list, clarifying one or two matters arising. There is also the issue of Dr. Baccard's exhibit which we have yet to resolve. I don't know if you want to address us on that then or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'd hoped not to be here myself on Friday. It's possible I will have to be. It depends on how the witnesses map out. And I can see some slippage of time this week already for reasons outside our control. So I might prefer not to be here on Friday if it could be dealt with either on Thursday or possibly next Monday. I'm anxious to revert to the witness list, and I'm having -- I'm taking steps in relation to both this part of the case and also the other part of the case to have lists prepared that will, I hope, be helpful for the Chamber and indeed for the accused because of his concerns about preparation over the summer. My forecast is that those lists will be available at about the end of the week but possibly not before. So that again would suggest a Friday hearing of these issues, or possibly Monday. We know that General Naumann's coming after Ambassador Walker, and I know that both men have got apparent time restrictions which I'm going to investigate when I go, when I leave the courtroom right now, but I think it's quite likely that the witnesses listed for this week will be difficult to squeeze in as it is, and there may be a small residue flowing over to next Monday in any event. I don't know if that helps. It probably only makes things more difficult. But if there's any chance of making the Friday hearing movable to allow the possibility, if all other things allow it and my not being here, I would be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can do that. We'll fix a suitable time. Perhaps you'd let us know how things are getting on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The Prosecution called Lutfi Ramadani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, I understand, sir, that you are a 58-year-old Muslim of Albanian ethnicity residing in Krusha e Vogel in Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you were originally born in the Suva Reka municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, how long have you lived in Krusha e Vogel?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: From 1958.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do I understand correctly, sir, that you are married and you have two surviving sons? Two other sons were killed on the 26th of March, 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, it may assist if I showed from the Kosovo atlas where Krusha e Vogel is. If you could turn to page 10. At -- if you look on the right-hand margin, number 23, and go immediately to the left to where at the top it says "70," you will see -- near where those intersect, you will see Krusha e Vogel. And perhaps we could just have the usher put this on the ELMO to have the witness point out where his village is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, if you would just look at that map and use the pointer and point out where your village is. Are you able to locate it?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You're pointing now to Prizren. Yes. Okay. You're now pointing to - yes - Krusha e Vogel. All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you also show the witness, please, two photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm going to show you some photographs, sir, aerial photographs. Do you recognise the village depicted in these aerial photographs? Mr. Ramadani, is that a photograph of your village?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll move on, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ramadani. I take it you're now pointing to -- is that a photograph of your village, sir?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ramadani, were you interviewed by members of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 20th of July of 1999, and did you give a statement on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you give two subsequent statements on the 26th of June, 2001 and the 5th of October of the same year, for a total of three statements?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you appear before a presiding officer of this Tribunal on the 4th of June of 2002 and have those statements read back to you and given an opportunity to make some corrections, if any?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And on that date, the 4th of June, 2002, after making some corrections, did you indicate to the presiding officer that those statements were true to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. I wonder, Your Honours, whether the package of materials under 92 bis might now be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 226.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I now propose to read a very brief summary of what is contained in that statement and follow that up with a couple of questions. Your Honours, as you will note from the various statements which have just been marked as exhibits, this witness indicates that at about 4.00 in the morning on the 25th of March, 1999, his family had left their house and hid in the woods due to the fact that the Serb police had surrounded their village. He indicates that at this time the police started to shell the village and later burned the Albanian houses. He describes that the Serb forces were wearing blue MUP, or police, camouflage uniforms. He describes in his statement seeing green-coloured APCs and tanks positioned around the village. He tells you in his statement that almost the whole population of the village were gathered in the woods, near a stream, close to a vineyard, where they stayed most of that day, that is, the 25th of March. At about 7.00 that night, the majority of them left that location and went to the house of Sejdi Batusha, due to the fact that it was cold and the young children were upset and crying. The witness and his entire family stayed at Sejdi Batusha's house until the following morning, the 26th of March, 1999. He indicates that the shelling continued until they were approached by a group of police, who told them to stay where they were or they would be killed. He says that he saw police take up positions on the roofs of some of the houses in that vicinity and that he observed Isen Kanjusha, who was not with his group, being shot. He states that the Serbs ordered Aziz Shehu to go to the woods and bring back those people who were still hiding there. In his statement, he then names the names of four men and four women who were brought back pursuant to that order, and indicates that all of those men are now deceased. He further tells you in his statement that the group was ordered out of the yard and onto the road, where the men were separated from the women. The women were ordered to go to Lake Vermica, and prior to leaving they were forced to hand over their personal belongings. He says that as the group of women were leaving, escorted by some police, he saw one of the policemen take several young boys out of the group and make them join the group of men. In his statement, you will find that when the women started to scream, they were threatened to be killed. At this point, the group of men were verbally abused by a policeman wearing a black mask, who was saying that someone else was going to have sex with their wives. He describes how the group of men were ordered to kneel down with their hands behind their heads for a considerable period of time and that Adem Isufi was ordered to go around to each man and collect documents, money, and car keys from them. This witness describes in his statement how the group was forced to line up in columns and were taken down the road in the direction of Qazim Batusha's cowshed or barn. He names some of the other victims who were with him. He describes that they were ordered into a two-roomed building with a central corridor and indicates that he stayed in the corridor because the rooms were too crowded. You will then read about how a policeman carrying a big machine-gun with a round ammunition box attached to it arrived, accompanied by other armed police. He then relates overhearing a conversation with other police who, in response to a request as to why the one policeman was late, indicated that "he would fix the problem in two minutes." The witness heard the sound of a gun being cocked, and almost immediately afterwards, the Serb with the machine-gun appeared in the doorway and the firing started. The witness fell to the ground and other villagers fell on top of him. The machine-gun firing stopped and he then heard the sound of single shots. He concluded that the victims who were not dead by machine-gun fire were finished with a single shot. He then tells you how he heard the sound of burning and saw bodies burning. The corridor filled up with smoke. He stood up and realised Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that there were others he knew who were still alive. He names those persons in his statement and describes his escape from the barn. In his 26th of June, 2001 statement he produces a map and refers to the house used as a barn, where over a hundred men and boys were shot and burned in this incident. He states that a crippled villager, Sait Hajdari, who was confined to a wheelchair, had been positioned by the Serbs in the doorway in order to stop the men from escaping the cowshed. This witness had to physically move Hajdari in order to escape. Having left the burning building, he and other survivors fled into the woods, shot at by police as he ran, and finally escaped. I now wish to turn, if I may, to two photographs. Mr. Usher, could you show the witness that photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ramadani, I ask you to look at that photograph. Can you tell the Court what that is a photograph of? I see you're having to put on your glasses. Yes. First of all, sir, do you recognise the scene depicted?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: This photograph is Bali Avdyli's house, and this is where the massacre took place. People were burnt and shot here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, for the record, sir, you're pointing to an area in front of what appear to be the remains of two buildings. Is the cowshed or the barn where this massacre took place, is that building still --

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Here -- it's not the shed here, but it was here, adjacent to the shed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. My question --

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Here it was mined. It was at this point. Here is where it was, where the shed was. It had two rooms and a corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, is what you are saying that nothing remains of this shed, but it's in the foreground, where you were pointing with your pointer?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Nothing remains, because when we returned from Albania, it was blown up, and there are only two holes here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. One final photograph I'd like to show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In your statement, sir, you refer to a wheelchair being positioned in the doorway. I'm going to show you a photograph now, if you would, please, and tell the Court if you recognise this particular photograph and what appears to be the remnants of a wheelchair.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: When they blew up the shed, they threw away this wheelchair.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How, if at all, does that wheelchair compare with the wheelchair that you saw on the 26th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: It's similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Who was the crippled individual in the wheelchair?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Sait Hajdari was in this wheelchair.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you recognise the lady depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I don't have a translation of the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the witness draw closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you speak into the microphone, please, Mr. Ramadani.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know this person. I knew Sait Hajdari, and that's what his wheelchair was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: My question is: Do you know the lady depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: No, I don't know this woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I don't know this woman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Remove the photographs, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Those are my questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You gave your first statement on the 18th and 20th of July, 1999, in Orahovac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And your second statement was given on the 26th of July, 2001; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: June. Correction.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did it come about that you had to give a second statement after giving the first one?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's be brief. And your third statement was given on the 5th of October, 2001. Your second one was given on the 26th of June, 2001, and the third one on the 5th of October, 2001; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I gave these statements, but I didn't write down the dates when I gave them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Why did you give three statements?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: When they came to see, themselves, we gave statements, and the people who were asked told what happened in Krusha e Vogel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Upon whose initiative was it? Who were these people that came to take your statement?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: It was my initiative to make a statement, and the people who came were investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why didn't you state everything that is contained in your third statement? Why didn't you say it when you were giving your first or second statement? Why isn't it contained in your first or second statement?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: My account is the same in the first, second, and third statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you read the third statement, you will see that the investigator gave the witness a map and clearly asked him to draw things on the map. In your first statement, were you asked - or your second - were you asked to draw on a map, Mr. Ramadani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He plainly doesn't understand. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And your third statement, was it taken down after what you said?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: These statements I gave were not given me to read, but they went to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your first statement, you said that you looked into the possibility of negotiating with the Serbs and that Ismail Arifi informed you that an agreement had been reached and that the Serbs would protect the Albanian population and the Albanians would protect the Serbs from the KLA. So this was an agreement among the residents of the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: They did make an agreement. I wasn't present. Ismail Arifi made the agreement with the Serbs. But they didn't keep the agreement. Those that made it did not keep it. The criminals of Krusha e Vogel who shot, burned 112 people, they shot 103 in one place --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We heard that, and that can be found in your statement. I would like you to concentrate on my questions alone now. Can you please tell me how many members of the KLA there were in Mala Krusa?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There was no KLA. It didn't exist in KLA [as interpreted]. Because there was a cafe owned by Nikolic which the police used as a station, and there the policemen beat and maltreated people. And even --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the cafe. Please answer my question. Just a minute ago you confirmed that an agreement had been reached and that the Serbs would protect the Albanians and the Albanians would protect the Serbs from the KLA. Now you're telling us that the KLA did not even exist. So how could an agreement have been reached for the Albanians to protect the Serbs from the KLA if the KLA did not exist? Why had an agreement been negotiated if there was no KLA?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I don't know why they made this agreement. I say that there was no KLA in our village. It didn't exist in our village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. You went on to explain something about this cafe owned by Nikolic, at which the police used to gather. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Even -- even children going to school carried weapons. And the police sat there in the cafe of Dimitrije Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And is it true that these Serbs, Petkovic called Nuci, Vuci Nikolic called Zivca, that you mention in your statement were in fact members of the local police or, rather, local security that had been established by the residents of Mala Krusa; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There were plenty of uniformed policemen there. They were almost all policemen. And I don't know how they were organised. Sometimes they were there, sometimes they were not. We didn't know who was a policeman and who was not; they all had uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you remember that there was a local security force in Mala Krusa consisting both of Albanians and Serbs and that there had been an agreement for the Serbs to protect their fellow villagers, Albanians, and vice versa, and to ensure that people could live in peace? Was it like that or wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The Serbs themselves were dressed as policemen, and even when foreigners --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, just concentrate, if you would, on the question. The question was: Was there an agreement in the village between the Albanians and the Serbs to protect each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was an agreement reached by some elderly people. And I was not present. I don't know how they did reach that agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now. It's time for the break. Mr. Ramadani, you're giving evidence. Would you please not speak to anybody until it's over about it, and that includes the members of the Prosecution. Could you be back, please, at half past eleven. We will adjourn until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a small digression, Mr. May. Yesterday, at the request of the other side, you asked that a document be returned to you from the set of documents that was given to me yesterday, so here it is, and the usher can take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the usher would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 25th of March, 1999, was there a clash between the KLA and the police?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why, then, did you seek shelter in the forest?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Because they attacked in the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who attacked houses?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that that police of yours that was in the village all the time that you've been referring to? Both Serbs and Albanians were on that police force. How is it that the police attacked houses?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: They were Serb police. There were no Albanian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. At that time when you went into the woods together with the other farmers, did the members of the KLA withdraw with you or not?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There was no KLA. Since there was no KLA there, how could the members of the KLA come there? There were women, elderly people, children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there were no men with them. The men were elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There were men. They were with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when you returned to the village around 1900 hours, as you had put it, were they with you then, the members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There was no KLA, but it was us, the people, with children, with women. All of us, we went to Sejdi Batusha's house. And there were people there. There were children under 15 years of age. There were 40 children there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you returned. You fled from the police, but you returned although the police were in the village. Why did you return if it's the police that you were running away from in the first place?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: We didn't leave. We didn't go far from the village. We just left the houses. We stayed near the stream, near the vineyard, near the village. And in the evening, it started getting cold. There were children. There were elderly people. There were girls. And the people started feeling cold. So did the elderly people. And then we went to the house of Sejdi Batusha. On that night, we stayed there. On the 26th, we woke up at 8.00, and at 8.00, they started setting fire to the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Please. You say that you returned to the village on your own and you went to Qazim Batusha's house, and in the statement you say that it was the police who forced you to enter the shed of Qazim Batusha; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: It was not a shed. It was a stable. They took us there. They executed the people and they set fire to them, 103 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I was talking about. And how many of you were in this group, all of you who were ordered to enter the stables?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There were 109 people. One hundred three people were left there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the livestock, was it in the stables or the barn, then?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: No, there wasn't. There wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. It was empty. And how many policemen were in the yard where the barn was?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There were about ten police who guarded us outside, and then there came the villagers there. Police of the village they were, Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, then: You say that a policeman appeared at the door of the cowshed and started shooting at you. Is that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: That police really came, and there was attached to him some other people. He was leading the other people. He entered the house and he started opening fire among the people. He executed the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know who Avdyli Mehmet from Mala Krusa is?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Avdyli Mehmet from Mala Krusa is my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he with you then in those rooms?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: He was there with me as well. There was also Mehmet Avdyli.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And do you know that he mentioned in his statement that it was not a cowshed at all, that it was a house? So where were you? Were you in the cowshed or were you in the house?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we have an interpretation, please.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: It was a stall, either a hall, not a house. Some people entered through the door with gun -- they opened fire against the people, and some entered through the windows. They executed all the people. They set fire to half of the people, and they were burnt half alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The witness has given his evidence about it. He says it wasn't a house. Now, the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many people survived this incident? Because you say that they killed everyone.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Only six people survived. All the people were executed and burnt, 103 people. We don't know where these people are buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you're the first one who came to the door and that you started to run away. Does that mean that you were standing by the door?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I was inside. I was among the dead people. And then I went out. I was on the right part, where the Serbs of the Krusha e Vogel were there. They were setting fire to the people. Then I observed that there were no people on the left part and it was possible for me to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If the policemen were around the cowshed, and if, as you say, they were setting it on fire, how did you manage to run away?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: God knows how I managed to run away. I am burnt, my clothes were burnt, and my right hand is burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did somebody else escape together with you in the same group or did you escape on your own?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There were six other people, two young boys, and after us, they were caught and executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And all of you escaped together, then, in that group, as you had described it?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: We were not all together, but we went as we could manage, just to save our souls.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A little while ago you said that you did not find the bodies of the persons who were executed. Did you see these people being killed?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I was among them. And it is true that they were killed. They were executed and then they were burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that these bodies that you assume were lost were burned down. Is that your claim?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, they were burned down. And what happened to their bodies, I don't know, because after the war, when we came back from Albania, that place was mined, and in that place we couldn't find anything but the shoes and the wheelchair of that person that I mentioned. There were other people who were crippled and couldn't move, and mentally ill people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that after that fire and after the killing, the place was mined and, therefore, you could not approach it when you returned?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: We find -- we found only some shoes and a wheelchair. The foundation of that house were blown up in the air. How did that happen? I am not aware of this fact because I was not present. About the mining, I don't know. You know it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, how far away was the asphalt road from which the other group shot at you?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The macadamised road is about 100 metres from the house, but they didn't shoot from the asphalt road. They shot from here, not from the asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From nearby. So they were from you -- they were shooting from two sides at you.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. About the place of the event where the people were executed and burned or you're speaking about another place?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I mean what you said in your statement. You say that the other group was shooting at you from the road as you were running away. So one group was shooting at you from the site that you had described, and the other one was shooting at you from the road. Does that mean that you were being shot at from two different sides?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I was being shot at from the place I came out of the house. I came out into the not-asphalted way. They shot at us, but, luckily, we were not killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So from how many sides were they shooting at you, from two sides, from three sides, from one side? From how many sides were they shooting at you?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: From there, we were three people. We were walking towards the road of Krushe e Madhe. They shot at us from the village and from the asphalt road until we entered the stream towards the mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they were shooting at you from two places; is that right? From two sides, that is. From the asphalt road and from the village itself.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Both from the asphalt and from the village itself they were shooting at us while we were leaving the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can that mean that from two sides -- from the two sides where the shooting was coming from, could that have been the police and the KLA, that they were shooting at each other and that you were caught up in the crossfire?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There was no KLA in the asphalt road, and there was no KLA in the village. But it was the Serbs of the village of Krusha e Vogel. They surrounded the place, the village; some were in the asphalt road and some were near the houses, from where they shot at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now you say the Serbs from Mala Krusa. So it's the Serbs, the villagers, who had set fire to their very own village. And a little while ago, you said it was the police who came in and set fire to the village. So who did it, actually?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Those people who destroyed the house, they destroyed the houses of the Albanians. They were only the houses of the Albanians looted by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Just give me a brief answer to the following question: If they were shooting at you from two sides, wouldn't they be shooting at each other that way as well?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I gave my answer. Those which I said, from the asphalt road and from the village. They didn't shoot against each other. The asphalt is down, and the village is in the side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since you mention in your statement the headquarters, is it true that the KLA was near that house that you refer to as the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There was no KLA in our village. There didn't exist even in the vicinity of our village such a KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But I'm asking you to clarify this which I do not understand. Why are you mentioning a house now whereas in your first statement you mention headquarters? Why the difference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Whereabouts is it in the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in these two statements. I can't waste time searching for it now in the statement, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you go on, you will tell us where it is. If you're going to put things to witnesses, they must have the chance of dealing with it properly. Now, you can tell us where this is or we'll go on to another question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is the witness denying the fact that he refers to headquarters in the first statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are not going to put things to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. witnesses without referring them to the statement and where it is. And then, no doubt, afterwards when you find it you claim there is some sort of bias. That's one of the sleights which you [Realtime transcript read in error "I"] use in cross-examination. Now, before you go on, if you want to ask this question, you must tell us where it is in the statement so we can check to see where it says. Then if it's a fair question, you can ask it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right. Obviously, now it is hard for me to find it in these three statements, but I will have it marked for you and then I'll give it to you. And I'll move on to my next question now, because, otherwise, I'll waste a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your second statement, you say that the Serbs removed the house and the mortal remains of the people who were there and that they threw them into the Drin River and that that is what you know. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I don't know about this fact because I was not present there when they shot. And I don't know what they have done with these.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If there are no witnesses concerning these events, does that mean that you are the sole witness of these events?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I am a witness about the fact that they were executed and burnt. The Serbs of Krusha e Vogel did these things with the help of the people from the neighbouring villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are there any other eyewitnesses?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you say their names? Who are these other eyewitnesses?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: They will come here and witness for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you give us their names, though?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There was mentioned here Mehmet Krasniqi. He is a witness here. Declares that the people were executed and burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
