utterances.text: All right. Do you know who Dimitrije Nikolic and Djordje Cvetkovic are?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, I know them very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. I've noticed a mistake in the transcript which is serious enough and should be changed. At line 21, it has me quoted as saying, "That's one of the sleights which I use in cross-examination." It should read, "That's one of the sleights which you use in cross-examination." The matter should be made plain. Yes. We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are they people from your own village?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: They are of our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And were they members of the local security that you had?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: We don't know, because at that time they were mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that in the village there were no members of the army. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The Serb army was at the asphalt road and in the vicinity. In the village, I myself didn't see. Perhaps there have been, but I didn't see with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that Nebojsa Nikolic - and you said that he was killed at Pastrik, as a reservist of the MUP - wore a green camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was a uniform, but he went as a volunteer. I knew this when I came back from Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But just now you told us that the army was not in the village but rather on the asphalt road. Does that mean that the army was outside of the village?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Perhaps it was also in the village, but for myself, I didn't see it. From where I was gathered with the population, I didn't see the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Will you please answer the question. Why did you state in your first statement that the village had been shelled and that this was the reason why you left your houses, whereas in the third statement you say that the artillery had not been used? How was the village shelled if the artillery had not been used?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: They fired from armoured vehicles, and they fired on my house, and the bullet is inside and was given to the investigator. I don't know where it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Was the artillery used or not, please? Just tell me that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where does it say the artillery wasn't used?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I'm asking him, Mr. May, to tell me whether the artillery was used or not. I just want an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The artillery was not used. They merely fired from armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fired from what?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: From the asphalt, at the Albanians' houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there some artillery fire coming from a larger distance? For example, mortars that were fired at the KLA? So not from the village but from the distance, was there firing directed against the police that was in the vicinity of the village? Was there a conflict there at all?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There was no conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In your municipality of Orahovac, do you know how many conflicts there were between the police and the KLA?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I don't belong to Rahovec municipality but to Prizren municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me change my question. Do you know how many conflicts there were in your municipality and in your vicinity between the police and the KLA?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I don't know of any conflict having taken place in our village or of the KLA being involved in any clashes, not one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about your area. Do you have any information of at least a rough number of the KLA members that got killed in the fighting with the police and the army?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: No. There was nothing of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your area, Prizren, and that part that is close to Albania, suffered intense bombing or was subjected to intense bombing. Do you know anything about the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There was no NATO bombing until the 26th. Around there, there wasn't any at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please: Do you know how many people in your area were killed as a result of NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Not a single person was killed by the NATO bombing, and nor did NATO bomb the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So if I understood you well, you claim that during those conflicts starting on the 24th of March, nobody got killed, no Albanian got killed as a result of NATO bombing, nor were there any people that were killed, any members of the KLA that were killed during fighting with the police or the army. Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has answered these questions. He has given his answer both about the KLA and about the NATO bombing. He's made that quite plain. Now, Mr. Milosevic, time is running out. Do you have any more questions of the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that means if no KLA members were killed in the fighting, if nobody was killed in NATO bombing, then everybody that was killed, as you claim it, were civilians, and they were killed by the Serb army and the police. Is that the gist of what you are telling us here?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Albanians were killed only by the Serbian police. That's in the village of Krusha e Vogel. Only the Serbian police, and also local villagers who joined them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And by trying to portray all of those who were killed as victims of the Serb police, do you perhaps try to cover up the fact that some of the people were killed as a result of the fighting and some of the people were killed as a result of the bombing? Please think carefully over this question and give me an answer.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: They were all shot by the Serbian police. They were shot, and 112 people were shot and burnt in one place; and in another, 103. This was the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Alongside with the village. Serbian villagers -- the Serbian villagers wanted to ethnically cleanse the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic, have you any questions, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ryneveld?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, two areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, in cross-examination, you were questioned as to whether or not you were sure that these people who you left behind in the barn were in fact dead. When you came back, you came back to your village of Krusha e Vogel?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: On the 4th of June, we came back. I think it was the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you have lived back in that village since the 4th of June of 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Have you seen any of those people who were in the barn with you, other than the ones who escaped with you, have you ever seen any of those people alive since?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I saw Mehmet Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's the only one?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I saw also Agim and Bajram.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And these are people that escaped with you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. These are people that escaped with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Other than the people who escaped with you, did you see any others alive since you returned?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: These 103 people remained there. They -- they are no longer alive. They were burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. One other area that I might ask you to try another look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you assist? Your Honours, I propose to show the witness photograph 0210321006, and I'm going to ask that he look at it before it goes on the ELMO, perhaps, to orient himself. This, Your Honours, is in relation to cross-examination about the route and the location of the asphalt road, to assist the Trial Chamber in terms of distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: First of all, sir, do you recognise -- you're looking at the photograph. It's an aerial photograph. Do you see the yard of Sejdi Batusha?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And before we put it on the ELMO, do you see the road leading to Qazim Batusha's barn, where it used to be? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Just a moment. Yes. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. All right. And then looking towards the top of the photograph, beyond the line of trees, there seems to be a horizontal line. Is that the asphalt road or is that something else?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: No. That road is not asphalted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: This is a dirt road.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Perhaps if you could put that on the ELMO now, you could explain to the Judges where Sejdi Batusha's yard was and where you walked to the barn location.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: This is Sejdi Batusha's house. This is where we stayed. And from here, they took us out onto the road and divided the men from the women and the elderly. And they told the women, "Go drown in the Drin if you like. Go to Albania if you like." Some children were with them --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking you to retell the story. I'm asking you if you would point out where the men were taken to the barn.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Right. From here. They separated us here. Women went over there, and we went along here to Qazim Batusha's front door. And we went in there. And that's where the shed is, in --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: -- middle between these destroyed houses and --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you've been shown a photograph where you say the foundation of what was the shed is still visible. Now, if you look at the top of the photograph, there is a line just beyond the trees. Do you see that line running across the -- no. Farther up. Point your -- farther. Farther up towards the top of the photograph. Top of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Here?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No. Sir --

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Here?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- do you see the top of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Here? Ah. Ah, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. What is that?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: This is -- this is the paved road. This is the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Is that the asphalt road to which you refer in your statement?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And finally --

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This is the asphalted road.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: One more question about this map, or about this photograph. You have described in your statement your route of escape. Go back to the location of the barn and show with the pointer, if you would, your route of escape, please.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: From here, we went out here. Along here, that's where my house is. And we went through here and through -- and we stopped a little bit here and then we went on. We went on down and came out on this road, this dirt road that goes to Krushe e Madhe. That's where that road is. And from the asphalt, they fired at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Those are my questions. I hope that assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Usher, as you escort the witness, could you please return with Mehmet Avdyli. Again, while we're waiting for the witness, Your Honours, the next witness describes the same incident. Therefore, I do not propose to show maps or photos to this particular witness, to save time. Just so you know we're talking about the identical incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Avdyli, do I understand correctly, sir, that you're 43 years old?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: No. I'm 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. I've got that information correct. You're of Kosovo Albanian ethnicity, are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And I understand you lived all of your life in Krusha e Vogel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How many children do you have?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: I have three; two sons and a daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you give two statements to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor; on the 4th of April, 1999, and then again on the 5th of October of 2001?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: Yes, I did make them on the 4th of April, but the second one, I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And just recently, on the 7th of March, 2002, did you appear before a presiding officer of this Tribunal and give a solemn declaration that the contents of those two statements were correct to the best of your information and belief?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might the statements which are attached, might those be marked as an exhibit in these proceedings, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: While those are distributed, I propose to read a very brief summary of what this witness has indicated in those statements. Your Honours, you will find that he indicates that the entire village of Krusha e Vogel, which to the best of his estimation has about 400 inhabitants, that they were all civilians, and there were both Serbs and Albanians living there, and they lived in relative harmony until after the airstrikes began by NATO on the 24th of March, 1999. He then indicates that on or about 3.00 a.m. on the 25th of March, 1999, Serb tanks entered his village. This event caused the villagers, including his wife and children, to flee to a nearby forest. He says that at daybreak, the Serb tanks fired for about an hour upon those people hiding in the forest. He saw that the MUP or police were taking away vehicles and tractors from the village and observed the village being progressively burnt down by the Serbs. At about 9.00 in the morning on Friday, the villagers were captured by the Serb forces. The men were separated from the women and children. The women were instructed to go to Albania and chased away. The group of men and boys totaled about 110, and according to the witness's statement, they ranged in age from 13 to 72 years of age. Apparently the group was searched, had their wallets and identity cards confiscated. He says that they were forced to kneel on the ground with their hands behind their heads and with their heads on the ground. If anyone raised their heads, they were subjected to severe beatings on all parts of their bodies. He then describes in his statements how the group was taken to the house of Haxhi Batusha where all of the 110 males were forced inside this two-bedroom house. Included in that group of 110 was a man who was an invalid and was confined to a wheelchair. He says that at the time, the house was intact and had not been hit by any shells prior to the group being forced inside. Once inside, they were subjected to abuse, and while being verbally abused, the Serb forces opened fire with firearms through the windows. At the completion of the shooting, he says he saw a policeman throw hay on top of the bodies and then set fire to the hay. He says not all of the victims were killed by gunfire but some of the survivors were subsequently incinerated by the ensuing fire. The witness then describes how he escaped the burning house and later observed the MUP officer stealing a motor vehicle owned by his uncle and that he saw how the police continued to feed the house fire with maize stems to intensify the fire. He says the village burned for the next few days. He fled to the forest and eventually received medical attention for the severe burns he suffered during the fire. While leaving Kosovo for Albania, he and two others were detained by the Serb police, tied to a heater, interrogated, and accused of being members of the KLA. In his statement, the witness provides the names and ages of the majority of persons killed during the execution at the house or barn of Mr. Batusha. That is a very brief summary. Obviously, I've left out many of the details. And I'm sorry, I didn't get the exhibit number for the statement while it was -- while I was reading in the summary, so I've delayed that. Might that be given one now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 227.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You gave your first statement in April of 1999 in Albania; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you give your second statement?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: In Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why was it necessary to give a second statement after giving the first one?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: Because it was necessary -- because it was a very tragic case in my village, when more than a hundred men, young boys and old men, lost their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you graduate from school?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you are working the land. You have been working the land ever since you started working; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was any member of your family a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement dated October 5th, 2001, you state that five of the residents of your village were members of the KLA, but they were not your relatives; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: They joined the KLA after the war, and before, there wasn't any KLA at all, and I never had any contact with the KLA. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you spoke of the time in the beginning of the war, and in your statement you said that five farmers were members of the KLA. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: No, that's not right. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And these people whose names you gave in your statement, do you know them well?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: Yes, I know them very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, when did they become members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: I saw them after the war in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When after the war?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: After we came back from Albania. This was very late, maybe -- I don't know what date, but it was very late, when anybody could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And who was the commander of the KLA unit to which these five farmers belonged?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't even speak to them about this sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In your statement April 4, 1999, you stated that everything was peaceful in the village until the NATO air raid started. Nothing special or particular occurred prior to that; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was your village bombed? I mean the village or the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: I didn't understand that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was the area around your village, including your village, bombed?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: What do you mean? When we were in the village or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Both when you were in the village and when you were outside the village.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: When we fled to the woods, there were gunshots. When the gunshots came, we fled to the woods immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: May I interrupt just for one moment? If Your Honours are looking through the bis'ing package, you'll see that the 5th of October statement is in fact missing. It's on its way. We have two copies of the -- I have a copy, but apparently the package that was handed in is missing that statement. So I just thought I -- it is on its way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I think we probably got copies from the original disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. I just didn't want the Court to be looking through the documents that were just handed in only to find that they're not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When I refer to the bombing, I am referring to bombing from aircraft, that is to say, throwing bombs out of an airplane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're talking about the NATO bombing; is that right? Is that what you want him to deal with?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want him to answer my question, whether he knows whether the area around his village was bombed and whether he saw that. I think that that is a perfectly clear question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Avdyli, the first question is this: Was your village or the area round about bombed by NATO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As long as I was in Kosova, it was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Then the question is: Was it bombed by anybody else, from the air?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There was the sound of machine-gun fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody bomb the village from the air?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: No. As long as I was there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that there was no bombing, and in the statement dated the 4th of April, on page 2, in paragraph 2, you say that you saw a Serb neighbour of yours turning off the light and taking his family into the cellar. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you also go to the cellar in your house with your family?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were not afraid of the bombing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: We were not scared by the NATO bombardment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that on the 25th of March, at 3.00 in the morning, you heard tanks going by your house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: Around the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: By the village. And did they enter the village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: Yes, they did enter the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when they entered the village, what happened when the tanks entered the village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: The people left. Once the tanks came into the village, the people left for the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that when dawn broke, that the tanks started shooting at the upper part of the forest, that the shooting went on for about one hour. Who were they shooting at, I mean the tanks, when they were shooting at the upper part of the forest?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: When they came, the forces of the army, we were up to the mountain, so they were shooting towards us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were in that part of the forest at which they were shooting from the tanks?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: We went towards the woods. We sought refuge in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand what you are saying. But if you say that they were shooting at you while you were in the woods, does that mean that somebody got killed by this fire coming from the tanks, somebody in the woods?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: I don't know about anybody being killed in the woods because of the tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what were these tanks shooting at, then?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: I don't know it even myself. They were shooting in the direction of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you were those people; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And nobody got killed?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there some other people there then when you say "these people" or "those people"?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This Friday that you're referring to was the 26th of March, 1999; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now explain something to me that I do not understand. You claim that you saw Serbs gradually burning the village on Friday, and further on in your statement you say that on Friday, at 9.00 in the morning, 15 policemen entered the woods and took you to Haxhi Batusha's house, an Albanian whose house is on the outskirts of the village, by the forest. This is in your statement dated the 4th of April, page 2, paragraphs 5, 6, and 7.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: There were 15 police who entered the woods, because on the 26th, they surrounded us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How big was Haxhi Batusha's house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: There were two rooms and a corridor. The house was one floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A total of two rooms; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: Yes. Two rooms and a corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that in these two rooms and in that corridor -- as far as I could understand it, actually, these rooms were four by four metres; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I haven't measured them. Perhaps it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you say 110 people managed to fit into these two rooms and that one corridor; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when the policemen started shooting at you, what time was it then?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I didn't have a wristwatch with me because we were robbed of the wristwatches. They took our wallets and everything we had in our possession. We were not allowed to have anything in the hands. We were forced to have our hands up above our heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they shooting at you through the doors and through the windows or only through the doors?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: In the room where I was, they were shooting at us through the windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Ramadani Lutfi testified here before you concerning the same event, and he said that you were not in a house. He said that you were in a cowshed. He said that the policemen were shooting from the door of the cowshed, and you say that you were in a house and that they were shooting at you through the windows. Can you explain this in somewhat greater detail? He was with you then; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can't give evidence about what somebody else said. Was this a house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give the statement of anybody else. I'm speaking about myself. I was there in that room, present, which had -- which -- and there was hay in that room. And what happened in the corridor and in the other room, I am not well aware about. Shefqet Shehu was standing on foot after the executions, and I have heard with my own ears that he said to the Serbs, "Are you doing so?" And then they shot again Shefqet, who was a student of chemistry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to draw your attention to page 2 of your statement, where you say -- it's at the very bottom of the page: "The entire group of men that numbered about 110 were crowded into two rooms of the house, four metres by four metres, squashed into two rooms of the house." That's why I asked you whether it was four by four. And you said that you hadn't measured it. So it was in these two rooms in that house. Now you say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. He also said that it could be true that it was four by four.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not the point. The point is that there is an enormous difference. Are we speaking about two rooms four by four in a house or are we speaking about a cowshed? I can't understand this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You are not here to make speeches. You will ask questions. If you have any more questions -- don't interrupt. If you have any more questions of this witness, you can put them to him. Meanwhile, you're not to make speeches now. The witness has said it's a house, and he's described it. He can't comment on what somebody else may have said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am addressing this comment to you gentlemen. We are listening to such fabrications here that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This isn't the time to address comment to us. If you are saying this witness has made up what he's told us about being present during an execution, you put it to him so that he can answer. If you are saying he's lying, you must put it to him about this sort of event.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I believe that both of them invented this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. It should be put to the witness in terms. You can't make these comments without giving the witness a chance to answer. What is being suggested, so you understand this, Mr. Avdyli, by the accused is that you have invented this story about being present in a house in which a hundred people were executed. Do you follow what he's putting to you, what he's suggesting? What's your answer to this? Have you made all this up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I couldn't make it up. Nothing could I make up. I have come here only to tell you the truth. Look how I am burnt in the two hands and in all of my face. I'm all burnt. I have these scars and signs here. I've come here to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The transcript should reflect the fact that the witness has shown the Court what appears to be the scarring on his wrists. Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Any more questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, within the time that I have available, I shall certainly put more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The windows that they were shooting at you from, did they face the same side of the yard or different sides of the yard?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: They were from the side of the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they faced the same side of the yard, these windows? How many windows did this room that you were in have?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: In the room where I was, there were two windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they shooting at you from both or through both or through one only?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: They were shooting from one window, which I saw with my own eyes. I've seen it with my own eyes from the window which looked at the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you say that you fell on the ground as soon as the shooting started.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And after that, they brought hay and they threw it all over you. Is that your assertion?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: They have burnt us. They put hay upon us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when they were throwing hay at you, did they enter the room that you were in?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: I couldn't see them because I was among the dead people and among the wounded people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they throw the hay in through the window or through the door?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: I didn't see how they threw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, how long were you in that room where you stayed with the dead?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: I don't exactly know how long I stayed here, but there were so many people blocked. They were wounded, severely wounded, and they had some slight wounds. There was one, Muharrem Asllani. He was my neighbour, and he had his arm cut by the machine-gun fire. He was blocked from the fire. So when they started spreading hay upon the dead people, I saw the -- I saw the people in blood. I could not be able to breathe because my blood became very thick because of the smoke. And I came out of the fire, and I said better die from the bullets rather than be burnt alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 3, in the middle, it says: "The group was forced into the house around 11.00, and I escaped at about 1500 hours, after the smoke became unbearable." And then further on, you say that you sustained burns to your face from the flames that still raged on the bodies. How is that possible? How can this room be on fire for several hours, the same room that you were in, and how could you survive that? How could you spend a few hours in these raging flames, as you had put it? Even four hours later. There was four hours between 11.00 and 1500 hours when you escaped, and flames were still raging. How was it possible for someone to spend four hours in raging flames regardless of whether he is believed to be dead or alive or just wounded or not wounded at all or even wrapped in something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, it's time there was a question. Mr. Avdyli, you've heard what is being put by the accused. Can you deal with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once more, I didn't understand the question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's understandable, considering how long it was. What appears is being put is that there was a fire, and you were able to stay in the room for several hours. How was that possible if there was a fire going on?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not that it was on fire. Raging flames, that's what it says here, at least in the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't -- I am not saying that I'm making up this story, but I don't know exactly how long I stayed among the dead bodies and among the fire. But since the dead bodies were blocked and Muharrem Asllani started crying that he was being burnt -- I don't -- I don't know how long I stayed there in that fire and among the dead bodies. So I came out of that place, and I say, "Better to die from the bullets rather than be incinerated," like many other people died being burnt, and I couldn't stand hearing their cries. I didn't have a wristwatch. As I said it, we were robbed of everything that we had with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So what you're saying, then, is that you might not have spent as long as four hours in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Really, I don't exactly know how many hours. I just know that I tried to escape and die from the bullets rather than from the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question is the following: How did you manage to escape since there were police around there? That's your claim.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: In that room, there were two windows, one window at the sides [as interpreted]. I didn't come out of that window from where they were shooting, which was siding the yard. I came out of the other window and between the house of my uncle, Bali Avdyli, and I entered the cellar of the house of my uncle. My uncle's house was near this house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. A while ago, in response to my question, you said that both windows were facing the same direction. Now you say that one window was on one side and the other window was on the other side. Please make up your mind. Did both windows face the same way or did the room have windows on both sides, on two different sides, and then you managed to escape through one of the windows? So what is the truth out of all that you have been saying?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: This is not true. You are planning it. I say that this room had two windows. The other one had one window, whereas the house had three windows and a corridor. One window was at the side and the other was opposite the yard. And it was not a big window; it was a small window.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The fact that it was a small window does not mean that it can be interpreted as an answer to the question that I put to you previously: Which side did the windows face, the same side or different sides?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given his answer, and it may not, considering the magnitude of what happened, as the witness said occurred, matter which side the window was. Now, Mr. Milosevic, technically you have another ten minutes. Have you more questions for ten minutes? If so, we'll adjourn. Or can we finish before lunch?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, after the break I can complete the remaining ten minutes. That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now. Mr. Avdyli, could you be back, please, at half past 2.00 to finish your evidence. Could you remember not to speak to anybody about it until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. We'll adjourn now until half past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we adjourn, I'd like the Prosecution to give us some clarification. I understand the witness changed name from Avdyli to Krasniqi after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: After the war. That's in his statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I noticed some various signatures which is in the bottom part of his statement, in Albanian and in English. And there are several. So what -- could you give us some clarification about that later? I don't think that they are all -- that's consistent, one writing. There's different writing. I notice there are some differences, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could perhaps report that after the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I condensed this, and I will fit within the ten minutes allotted to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did you manage to enter the house of your uncle since the policemen were obviously in the yard of your uncle's house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: I entered from the lower part, from a door that is down below. And I used a baby's nappie, and I wrapped my hands in that, but sometimes they went round the side of the house. And then there was Sveta Tasic, from our village, who took my uncle's car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, how did you then manage, and at what risk, to escape from your uncle's house if the policemen were still there? Were the policemen still there when you fled into the forest or had they already gone at that time?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: As long as I was there, I went also up to the second floor where I saw the village -- the Serbs of the village who were still throwing hay on top of the bodies. There was Slavisa Petkovic and Boro Stankovic who were throwing hay on top of the bodies. And I saw this from the place where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you how did you manage to flee once again from your uncle's house into the forest if the policemen were still there? Did you wait for the policemen to leave or did you flee with them still there? How did you manage to flee? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: I stayed there until late, until the evening. And after it got Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. dark, I went down to the stream and then up into the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And were they still there when you were trying to flee or had they already gone at that time?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: All day -- they were there all day. I saw them in my uncle's cellar. I saw them all there. I saw the sons of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but as you were fleeing, as you were leaving, as you were fleeing into the forest.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: Just a moment. When I fled to the forest, there was none of them left. Because if they had been there, I would have been a dead man. I didn't seek shelter there, but I went there by chance, thinking that perhaps they wouldn't come there, because they had searched all the houses in the morning, and they had ransacked them and thrown all the clothes about and the contents. And they did that in my uncle's cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. Thank you very much. I can see that you are saying untruths again. I want to point the penultimate paragraph on page 3 to you when you explain how you left your uncle's house, where you say: "I withdrew into the forest where I stayed until midnight, looking at the house in which there were dead people, and the policemen were feeding the fire until late into the night," whereas now you claim that they'd already gone when you fled. Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: In the evening, they withdrew and stayed in the houses where they were staying. And then when I went out, I didn't see any of them because it was night, and I didn't see any policemen round about. If I had seen one, I would have been a dead man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. It is quite clear, quite clear. In your second statement, you said that you did not see the vehicles nor the weapons from which they were shooting, and you said that they were shooting above your heads. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: What do you think -- I don't understand this question very well. What place are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you said while you were in the forest there was artillery firing directed at you, that you saw artillery pieces firing at you. Didn't you say that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: Yes. That was before, when the people were sheltering in the forest. That's when they fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. Prior to that, you said that you saw artillery firing at you. And let me read to you what your statement contains. This is paragraph 6 on page 1, or rather, on page 2, because the first page is always a cover page, and I'm reading verbatim: "I did not see either the vehicles or the weapons because they were shooting towards the forest above our heads. They used heavy artillery. We heard detonation as they were firing, and one tree was cut into half by a shell." This is the entire paragraph. So what is the truth here: what you said before the break or what is contained in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: That was on the 25th, when they fired on the population in the village -- in the forest, not the day when I went out into -- not the night when I went out into the forest myself. I'm talking about the night later, on the 26th, when I went to the forest. I was injured, with all my hands and face burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I am referring to the 25th, because that is the only incident that you described that they fired at you while you were in the forest. But what is the truth here: what you said before the break or what is contained in your statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't remember any discrepancy between the two. You're referring here -- you were asked by the investigator, I suppose: I have been asked if I know what types of weapons were being used by the Serbs to fire upon the civilians from the villagers who were hiding in the woods. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They fired from below, where they were positioned, with their military hardware. They fired from below up into the forest, on the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I would like to remind you that this witness said here that they fired from the armoured personnel carriers and that there was no artillery, but rather, that they were shooting from machine-guns. This is what he said during his testimony here. And I would like to remind you here that he did not see APCs, that heavy artillery had been used, and that one shell even cut a tree into half, and that they were shooting above their heads. So this is a completely different description of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So let me continue. You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your time is now virtually up, but the witness should have a chance to deal with what you allege is a discrepancy. Now, is there any discrepancy in what you've said about the artillery or not? Was there artillery used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 25th, when the forces took position, we were in the forest, and then they fired artillery of various kinds. Shells fired from below us when we were in the forest and a tree was cut down there. And on the 26th, in the evening, I fled to the forest. Because when we were in the forest, we couldn't actually see the hardware they were using, though we knew where they were positioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask one more question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like you to grant three more minutes to me, because you took up some of my time. I planned this out carefully for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, can you tell me who dictated the persons of these people that were allegedly killed? Did you know them, and how did you acquire information on their years of birth, and under whose instructions did you invent this description of events? What was promised to you in exchange for this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is a series of questions in that, one of which is a suggestion that this witness has made up his evidence yet again, the suggestion made again. Now, Mr. Avdyli, this will be the last question you are asked, because there are two or three questions in it. First of all, in your statement you have listed those who were executed. What is suggested is that this was dictated to you. Now, can you tell us how you came to list those who were executed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were all from my village. They were all people I knew from my village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The list contains, it's pointed out, the various ages. Where did you get the ages from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We got them because I knew, more or less, roughly, how old they were, because I was born there in that village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, it's suggested that you've invented this, indeed all your evidence. What's your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I haven't invented this at all. I haven't done this myself. I haven't written this myself. I haven't imagined this. I knew all these things, and I knew how old these people were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Has the amicus got any questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask another question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. You've had your time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to kindly ask you to just clarify this issue that had been brought up already by Honourable Judge Kwon. I would like to ask Mr. Krasniqi, or rather, sorry, Mr. Avdyli: I know Albanians frequently change their last name, and can you tell us what was the reason for your changing your name in such a short period of time?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: It wasn't for a reason. The thing is that my father and brother used the surname Krasniqi, and my father has now died, and my brother is Krasniqi. But nevertheless, my documents were in Avdyli, so I wanted to have the same name as my brother because I couldn't find these old documents. And now at UNMIK, my documents are registered in the name of Krasniqi, my entire family.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, why were you brought here under the last name of Avdyli if your current last name is Krasniqi, in fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not his responsibility. It's the responsibility of those who took the statement. Now, Mr. Tapuskovic, if there's some point in this we will continue, but there doesn't at the moment seem to be any point in it. He's explained why he's changed his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to explain the difference in his signature when he signed his name as Mehmet Avdyli - this is on the 4th of April of 1999 - and his signature on the statement from March 2002, 7th of March, 2002. I would simply like the witness to explain this. I have no further questions. I would simply like the signatures to be shown to him so that he can explain it. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is there to explain? His name was Avdyli. He signed that in 1999. And then he's Krasniqi later on. What is it that you want him to explain, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If it assists, Your Honour, I believe the question is that the signatures appear to look different. I have a question that might clarify that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And I also have a photo, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let counsel for the Prosecution deal with it, then. Mr. Tapuskovic, we will let the Prosecution deal with it. They took the statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you wish me to do it now? Did we want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's what I think too. That's right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: With respect to your signature, quite apart from the fact that you signed one statement with the name Avdyli and the other with the name Krasniqi, you've explained that, there appears to be on your statement, sir, a difference in the type of handwriting. What I'm asking you now is: On the 3rd and 4th of April, were you suffering from any burn wounds to your hands as a result of what occurred to you on the 26th of March?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: Yes. My hands were very badly burned. They were entirely burned. They were all burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: As a result of medical treatment which you sought, were your hands bandaged? Were they wrapped with bandages?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you sign the first statement on the 4th of April with bandaged hands?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: Yes. I had bandaged hands. That's how I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did the bandages on your hands affect your ability to write as legibly as you might do two years later?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: Not just a bit. At that time, it was very difficult for me to write at all because I couldn't hold a pencil.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, if that clarifies the matter. I do have a photo from the Internet showing bandaged hands, but I don't know whether that's necessary, given his answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure this is of great importance, but let's put it simply. Could the usher put this witness statement on the ELMO. Mr. Krasniqi, could you kindly look at the signature at the bottom of the page. That's the English version taken in 1999, and there's two signatures there. The bottom part. The signatures. There are two signatures. You recognise them? Who did this signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's my name and signature, name -- that is me. This other one, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And this time, Mr. Usher, could you put this on the ELMO. This is perhaps the third -- second statement, yes. There's some different handwriting. "Mehmet Krasniqi." You wrote this also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Mehmet Krasniqi"? Yes, I wrote that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You wrote that yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I wrote it myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And this time this is the signature that appears on the Albanian version. The left side. Yes. You also signed this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So all of them are done by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I do have one more question in re-examination, but I don't know whether Mr. Tapuskovic was finished. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: One more question, sir. You've been cross-examined about the house --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- where you were. You've described to us that in one of the rooms in which you were there was hay; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: That's right. In that room where I was, it was -- it had this -- it had hay inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you notice any furniture or any sign that it was being used for people to live in?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: No. This was an uninhabited house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET AVDYLI
utterances.text: It -- they -- they had filled it with hay and things for cows and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That clarifies my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Avdyli, thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. It's now over. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well, Your Honour and everybody, for making it possible for the blood of these people who died and make to the truth known to the world. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before the next witness comes in, two matters. First, may I shortly and respectfully just invite the Chamber to give thought to the following in relation to the manner of cross-examination of witnesses of the type we've seen over the last few days. If the witnesses are telling the truth, then cross-examination, to the effect that they fabricated everything, adds insult to injury and may be particularly distressing, perhaps even more distressing to people from this culture than from others. And I just wonder, and as I say, I'm asking the Chamber to think about it if it would -- if it could, I just wonder if when the accused makes this kind of allegation he should be required to make it clear whether he's doing it on the basis of material, he has witnesses who can support these allegations, or whether he's simply making it on the basis of what he can make of what's in a statement. Not only might this be of significance in the way the witnesses themselves are dealt with, but of course if in due course at the end of the trial we come to the position of finding that these allegations are -- that have been made are entirely groundless, it will be too late to do anything about it and we will have forgotten all about it by then. And I just wonder if the Chamber might think about it as a way of confining cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course if this were a -- not a litigant in person but somebody who was represented, we would expect matters to be put more accurately. Unless something is put, we will assume that it is merely an allegation. But it's right that the witnesses should have a chance to deal with it if it's being put, and it should be put fairly and squarely to them --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I entire agree. I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- so they can respond. Before we call the witness, there is something which I want to deal with. I should have mentioned it earlier. I was talking about clarification of the witness list, and there are two matters which possibly I should raise now because they concern witnesses who it may be, because we're going at a faster rate, could be called fairly soon. The first is Mr. Vllasi. We have considered his evidence or, rather, the summary that we've had of his evidence. We note that since he was not an original witness, you will require leave to call him. We, at the moment, are concerned about the -- given the number of witnesses and the amount of evidence, we are concerned that this is not of great relevance, and we will not be minded to give leave at the moment. It may be you'd like to reflect on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's very helpful to have that advance indication. If I can come back to you about it first thing in the morning, I'll let you know what my then-position is. I know that I had the intention to take his evidence shortly. I'll see if what's contained within the short passages I wanted to lead is worth drawing to your attention specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we ought to be considering these matters as to the amount of evidence. General Naumann we have also considered. Again, you'll need leave to call him, but clearly he's an important witness who deals with other matters, and we would be minded to give leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There may be some matters arising as to disclosure, about the time available, and it may be you'll have to make an application in respect of that. (redacted)- I may have got the name the wrong way around - he is, I think if I recollect, a verifier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can just remind you that there was another issue arising yesterday that we have yet to resolve. In fact, they're the same issue, I suspect. There's the issue -- it's a Rule 70 issue and it relates to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let me say, then, in relation to that, that we're not minded to be persuaded that the matters raised should be -- would be appropriate. I hope that makes it plain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I think this is touching on a sensitive area, and it may be appropriate for me to ventilate the topic a little more generally, perhaps in a private session, but not now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. But that's our view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, it's very helpful to have that view, and I'll communicate it to the government concerned. Of course, he's in the process of deciding on what representations to add to the material I've already laid before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we deal with the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Again, before he comes -- incidentally, in relation to (redacted), as I understand Your Honour's observations, this was nothing to do with dates of disclosure; it was simply in relation to the Rule 70 issue itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I can satisfy you, I think, about disclosure, but it's all wound up in the same general topic, and a rather complex history, so for another date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The immediately forthcoming witness, Ambassador Walker, I hope the Court has had an opportunity of considering --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question regarding the previous one, regarding the previous one, the previous issue that was mentioned. Can we receive the order of the witnesses today, the order of the witnesses after Walker? I take it that Mr. Walker will be the first witness coming, and can we have the order for at least the following week?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the order is being published and furnished to the defendant on the regular basis, and I don't know when the last one went out. The 7th of June is the date of the last one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And that is the current order --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the current order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- for next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Subject, of course, to deletions that the Court may make in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if things change, as they do from time to time, I make a point of notifying the accused at the earliest possible moment, where necessary getting messages sent to him in the late afternoon, if it is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ambassador Walker. I trust the Chamber has had the 92 bis package, as we are for some reason now calling it. It's not a package; it's a clip really, which contains the two statements in reverse order as to date, and the summary. The summary is the summary of the evidence that I would wish or feel obliged to give viva voce in any event, even if the Rule 92 bis application were to be granted in part. I can identify the paragraphs that would be taken live and would ask the Chamber to consider admitting the balance of the statements 92 bis, given that they cover materials covered by other witnesses, in particular, General Drewienkiewicz, and others. I dare say, in the nature of things, it's likely that the whole statement will go in under another route in any event and in due course, but to be sure, I should apply for the document to go in under 92 bis so that its status is clear. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's both statements you're asking to go in under 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you're asking, in fact, that only part of the statements go in. Those parts which deal with meetings with the accused you will deal with anyway, and I see you'll be covering Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely. Not all of Racak, but all that, it seems to me, new and significant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Racak is a topic which has been covered. The rest of his evidence concerning the Verification Mission and the background is cumulative, repetitive. We've heard other evidence about it, and therefore it comes within the Rule. However, we'll hear any applications that anybody wants to make. Mr. Milosevic, what is proposed should happen is that the statement of this witness should be exhibited and admitted under the Rule, but that he would be called to give evidence about some of the incidents in Racak, and particularly about any of his meetings with you, which doesn't come within the Rule because it relates to the acts and conduct of the accused, but that the other part should be admitted. You will, of course, have the opportunity to cross-examine. Is there any objection to our admitting the rest of the statement? No doubt you'll be cross-examining on it anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do object, because the witness was announced as a live witness, and now including his written statement in an indirect way limits the scope of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. It doesn't limit the scope of your cross-examination. Provided it's a proper cross-examination, you may cross-examine him on his statements. So the scope is not limited.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, so the time for cross-examination will not be limited either; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That is another issue which we'll come to in due course. But meanwhile, we'll admit the statements under Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness come in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness would take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your full name, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM GRAHAM WALKER
utterances.text: William Graham Walker.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Walker, is it right that you were a career diplomat in the United States of America, achieving the rank of ambassador, a rank in which you were confirmed by the Senate, thus giving you for life the entitlement to the title of Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM GRAHAM WALKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you now retired from work for the United States Department of State; you're vice-president of an international energy company?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM GRAHAM WALKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From August 1997 and until February 1998, were you the United Nations Transitional Administrator for Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM GRAHAM WALKER
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: UNTAES, I think, is the --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM GRAHAM WALKER
utterances.text: UNTAES.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: UNTAES. Thank you. Then, from the 17th of October 1998 and until mid-June of 1999, with rank of Ambassador, were you head of the Kosovo Verification Mission within the Organisation for Cooperation and Security in Europe?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM GRAHAM WALKER
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The KVM, as we know it to be called, being set up immediately following the OSCE-FRY agreement of the 16th of October, sometimes referred to as "the Holbrooke Agreement" because of the involvement of Ambassador Richard Holbrooke?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM GRAHAM WALKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to make any more of the background of this witness, which is contained within the materials. I can take the Court to the relevant paragraphs which underlie the summary paragraphs. The second statement is the first one in the bundle. The first one is towards the back. And paragraph 66 of the second statement can be found on page 35 of that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we given the statements exhibit numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We haven't. The whole package should be exhibited, please. And I think outstanding from yesterday is the request for clarification as to whether exhibits contained in these clips of documents automatically fall to be part of the exhibit when we produce the statement, even if the exhibit is not specifically referred to in the oral testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think that must be right, but it's sometimes more convenient if the exhibits are produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If they're looked at separately, yes. But of course, if the Chamber goes back to look at a 92 bis statement, which it's entitled to do, for its content, and then wishes to consider an exhibit, the exhibit has to be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's part -- unless I'm otherwise advised, it's part, it seemed to me, of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're grateful for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be given Prosecutor's Exhibit 228.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ambassador, I see you have open before you some documents. It may or may not be you'll be allowed to look at them. Perhaps you had better tell us what they are first and whether you need to refer to them, because the preference of the Chamber tends to be for people to speak without reference to notes when they can.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM GRAHAM WALKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have compiled what I call a chronology of events that took place during my experience in Kosova, and I have it more or less just so that I can remind myself of dates and people who might have been at meetings I attended, that sort of thing. The other package I have is my two statements that I've given to the Court, my sworn statements that I was given copies of yesterday when I signed them and swore to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Refer to them as you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your first meeting with the accused was in your role as a transitional administrator. When was it and what were your initial and first impressions?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM GRAHAM WALKER
utterances.text: The first meeting was from UNTAES. When I first took over UNTAES, I went first to Zagreb and met with Tudjman, and I believe it was on November the 18th of 1997 I flew to Belgrade and was received by then President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In a few sentences, because time is limited, but in a few sentences, give us your initial impressions and tell us how he dealt with you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM GRAHAM WALKER
utterances.text: It was what I would describe as a friendly meeting. He welcomed me, told me he was -- had heard about me, was -- told me that we were on the same side of the issues in Eastern Slavonia, that I was there to protect the Serb population from what he described as the possible intrusion by the Croats, and he told me that a General Loncar, who I think I had already met, he told me that he was there to work for me, that we, as I say, were on the same side of the issues. The meeting was informal. It was just him and a few of his people, me and a few of my people, very little of the formality that I had encountered with my meetings with President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
